newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin probes officials' wealth, scandals go on.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin probes officials' wealth, scandals go on.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin unveiled a new weapon on Friday in his declared battle against deep-rooted corruption, signing a decree forcing senior Russian officials to declare their wealth.

As Yeltsin made the announcement in a regular radio address, the military prosecutor's office was said to have laid corruption charges against Deputy Defence Minister Konstantin Kobets, once the Kremlin leader's close ally.
Russian media also reported new details indicating graft on a grand scale in the upper reaches of the armed forces, extending even to indiscriminate murder

"We have no illusions. We won't be celebrating a final victory over corruption any time soon," Yeltsin said, conceding the difficulty of stamping out a scourge that has afflicted Russia since tsarist times and throughout the Soviet years.

His new measure, part of a broader clean-up scheme launched when the president brought a number of young reformers into the cabinet in March, will oblige senior officials from himself downward to declare their income and assets every year.

"My task is to put an end to the situation when a state post serves as a source of enrichment," the president said. "Honesty today is not only a moral category. It has become a political category. People are tired of slogans and promises."
It is not, however, the first time he has launched a drive against corruption, so far with little result.
Graft charges, let alone convictions, have been very few.

In a rare case to surface recently, a reformist ex-adviser to Yeltsin, Sergei Stankevich, is awaiting extradition from Poland on a relatively modest $10,000 bribery charge. He was arrested shortly after Yeltsin launched his latest crackdown. Stankevich's lawyer says the Kremlin is seeking a scapegoat.
No-one doubts there are bigger fish to be netted.
Interfax news agency quoted an aide to the chief military prosecutor as saying Kobets, 57, had been charged on Friday with corruption and abuse of power.
The prosecutor's aide said charges had been laid after a long investigation into illegal dealings between some Defence Ministry officials and private Russian firms.
Officials were not available for comments. Kobets, who is in hospital after a mild heart attack, could not be reached.

Kobets, who has denied all allegations since they were first leveled by a lawmaker in the Russian parliament last summer, has been close to Yeltsin since leading the soldiers who defended him during the hardline communist coup of 1991.

The general, who had headed the crackdown on a bloody hardline revolt against Yeltsin in 1993, survived a Kremlin purge last year, when several hawkish aides including the defence minister, General Pavel Grachev, were ousted amid unsubstantiated allegations of corruption.

Chief Military Prosecutor Yuri Dyomin told Izvestia daily on Friday that 20 generals and admirals and 100 colonels were under investigation -- a situation made all the more scandalous by the sorry state of the lower ranks, who are going hungry, deserting and committing suicide in unprecedented numbers.

The civil prosecutor's office confirmed reports that three Afghan war veterans, including intelligence colonel Valery Radchikov, were charged with murder on Thursday over the bombing of a Moscow funeral last November which killed 14 mourners.
Rivalry between veterans' groups mixed up in corrupt abuse of tax concessions appears to have been behind the blast.
Yeltsin's latest decree, the brainchild of First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, was broadly welcomed even by his opponents in the communist-dominated parliament.
But many felt it would do little to stem the haemorrhage of cash from Russia's vast resources into the pockets of the well-placed few. Checking the declarations will be difficult.
And, though Yeltsin said he would shortly publish details on his whole family, relatives of officials are only "recommended" to make such declarations under to the decree.
